clue.text: Movie drug-runner meets bar owner in Ireland

definitions.note: the definition names a place found in Ireland, a city and county there

parts.note: Harry Lime, the racketeer selling diluted penicillin in the film The Third Man
Rick runs Rick's Café Américain in the film Casablanca

explanation.surface: A film villain who smuggles drugs teams up with a publican on the Irish scene.
explanation.walkthrough: Both pieces are film characters: Harry Lime of The Third Man and Rick of Casablanca. The definition is loose, standing for a place in Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Limerick is a city and county in the west of the Republic, so it is a place located in that country.

indicators.note: about here means moved around, so the letters of cagey are rearranged

explanation.surface: A Liberal politician is evasive about a bequest.
explanation.definitionFit: A legacy is money or property left to someone in a will, a bequest.

indicators.note: almost means the word for stingy loses its final letter

parts.note: mean means stingy, unwilling to spend
sly means cunning

explanation.surface: A cunning miser is offering a pitiful sum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' cuts MEAN to MEA.
explanation.definitionFit: Measly is informal for contemptibly small or meagre.

clue.text: One getting up in the middle of a flight

definitions.text: in the middle of a flight

explanation.surface: Someone stands up mid-journey on an aeroplane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flight' suggests an aircraft but means a flight of stairs; the upright part of each step is called a riser.
explanation.definitionFit: An early bird is someone who rises from bed; on a staircase the vertical board of each step has the same name.

indicators.note: cooked suggests something mixed up and changed, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A cattleman has prepared a stew.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cooked' rearranges COWHERD.
explanation.definitionFit: Chowder is a thick soup, usually of fish or clams, so a kind of stew.

explanation.surface: Ruining a drink, perhaps by spilling it.
explanation.definitionFit: To spoil a plan is to put a stop to it, as in scotching a rumour; whisky from Scotland is also a drink of that name.

parts.note: motor is a familiar word for a car
a race is a people, as is a nation

explanation.surface: A blunder occurs during a motor race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloomer' looks like a mistake but means a flower, something that blooms.
explanation.definitionFit: A carnation is a garden flower, so it is something that blooms.

parts.note: a temp is a temporary or casual worker
late means former, as in the late president

explanation.surface: A temporary worker's previous fashion model.
explanation.definitionFit: A template is a pattern used as a guide for making copies.

clue.text: Anglo-Saxon rebel, present on a charge

parts.note: here means present, as when answering a roll call
a ward is a person in someone's care, a charge

explanation.surface: An English rebel appears in court on a charge.
explanation.walkthrough: Hereward the Wake led resistance against the Norman conquerors in the Fens. 'charge' is a person in one's care, not an accusation.
explanation.definitionFit: Hereward the Wake led English resistance to William the Conqueror around Ely.

parts.note: a grass is British slang for an informer, someone who squeals to the police
to box is to punch, and a box on the ears is a blow

explanation.surface: An informer's blow slices through some container.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cutting' looks like a verb but describes clippings: the box on a lawnmower collects the cut grass. GRASS is British slang for an informer.
explanation.definitionFit: On a lawnmower, the catcher collects the clippings, so it is a container for cuttings.

indicators.note: the leading letter of the word Polish is the one wanted here

parts.note: a rimer (rhymer) is someone who writes verse

explanation.surface: A top Polish poet turns out a schoolbook.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leading Polish' suggests a famous Pole, but 'Leading' just takes the first letter, P. 'Polish' has a capital P only because it begins the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A primer is an elementary schoolbook that teaches the basics of a subject.

indicators.note: contains signals the answer is held within the letters of sherbet

explanation.surface: A fizzy sweet includes natural flavours.
explanation.definitionFit: Herbs such as basil or thyme are plants used to season food.

clue.text: Poet in pass by English hill range

parts.note: a col is a mountain pass, a dip between peaks
a ridge is a long chain of hills

explanation.surface: A poet walks through a mountain pass near some English hills.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Taylor Coleridge was the Romantic poet who wrote The Rime of the Ancient Mariner.

clue.text: Admit pasty lacks a bit of seasoning

indicators.note: lacks says the word for pasty goes without a piece named next

parts.note: a pasty complexion is pale and sallow

indicators.note: a bit of seasoning means just its first letter is taken

explanation.surface: Someone confesses that their pasty is missing some seasoning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pasty' is the adjective (pale), not the Cornish pie. SALLOW loses its S, the first letter of 'seasoning', which is what 'lacks a bit of' signals.
explanation.definitionFit: To admit someone is to let them in, so it means permit entry.

clue.text: Sign of damage to small vehicle

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a car is a vehicle

explanation.surface: A dent shows that a little car has been in a bump.
explanation.definitionFit: A mark left on skin or a surface after an injury shows where harm was done.

indicators.note: about places the word for concern around the word for the god's

parts.note: care is concern or worry
Thor's, belonging to the Norse god of thunder

explanation.surface: Worry over a god's beast of burden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Concern about God's' reads as worry over a deity, but 'about' is a container signal wrapping the first word round the second.
explanation.definitionFit: A heavy horse bred to pull carts is a draught beast used for labour.

clue.text: Skin problem in book by famous surgeon

parts.note: Joseph Lister, the British surgeon who pioneered antiseptic surgery

explanation.surface: A rash is described in a famous surgeon's memoir.
explanation.walkthrough: Joseph Lister was the Victorian surgeon who introduced antiseptics.
explanation.definitionFit: A raised bubble of fluid under the skin, caused by rubbing or burning, is a common complaint.

clue.text: Minister to watch, initially over utopian resort

indicators.note: in a down clue, over places one piece above, so before, the next
initially means only the first letter of watch is used
resort read as re-sort means sort again, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A clergyman watches over a holiday resort that seems like paradise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minister' looks like a noun but is the verb, to attend to. 'resort' reads as re-sort, signalling the anagram of UTOPIAN.
explanation.definitionFit: To wait upon someone is to serve them, to attend to their needs.

indicators.note: badly treated suggests something knocked out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Mistreated incomers are left in pain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Badly treated' rearranges MIGRANTS.
explanation.definitionFit: Smarting means stinging with pain, physical or emotional.

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A physician who has wed is someone's sweetheart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' reads as a noun but is a verb signalling the anagram of MARRIED.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who adores another person, a fan or suitor, is a devotee.

clue.text: Garment for Bishop of York turned up

indicators.note: in a down clue, turned up means read from bottom to top, so backwards

parts.note: Ebor is the signature of the Archbishop of York, from the Latin Eboracum

explanation.surface: A vestment for the senior cleric of York has arrived.
explanation.walkthrough: The Archbishop of York signs as Ebor, from Eboracum, the Roman name for York.
explanation.definitionFit: A robe is a long loose gown, a piece of clothing.

clue.text: Carol resides in either half of prison

indicators.note: either half means only one of the two identical halves of the jail's name is kept, here the front one

parts.note: ... ... is a famous maximum-security jail in New York State

explanation.surface: A girl called Carol lives behind bars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carol' looks like a woman's name but is the verb. Sing Sing, the New York jail, has two identical halves, so either one gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To carol is to chant joyfully, especially Christmas songs.

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for son
lavish means extravagant or excessive

explanation.surface: A boy is fawning to an extravagant degree.
explanation.definitionFit: Slavish means servile, showing excessive deference.

clue.text: Piece of armour protecting one old Roman procurator

indicators.note: protecting places the armour word around the letter, shielding it

parts.note: plate is a sheet of metal armour
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Armour shields a lone Roman official.
explanation.walkthrough: 'protecting' puts PLATE around I.
explanation.definitionFit: Pontius Pilate was the Roman governor of Judea who presided at the trial of Jesus.

clue.text: Fearsome woman is to get on without public relations

indicators.note: without means the letters for public relations are taken away

parts.note: to progress is to get on, advance

explanation.surface: A formidable woman must advance without a publicity team.
explanation.definitionFit: An ogress is a female ogre, a monstrous or frightening woman.

clue.text: Light from the church beyond the hill

indicators.note: beyond places the church's letters after the hill's, further along

parts.note: a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: A lamp shines from the chapel over the hill.
explanation.walkthrough: A tor is a rocky hilltop, common on Dartmoor in south-west England; 'beyond' means the church comes after the hill in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A flaming brand or hand-held lamp gives illumination.

indicators.note: finally picks the last letter of succumb

parts.note: ranging means roaming or wandering about

explanation.surface: In the end someone gives in to a wandering player on the wing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'winger' suggests a footballer but means a bird: the brambling is a finch.
explanation.definitionFit: The brambling is a finch, and a bird is something with wings, hence a flier.

indicators.note: restricting means the word for boom hems in the letter

parts.note: a boom is a spar or beam

explanation.surface: A barrier boom across a river keeps fish in.
explanation.definitionFit: Bream is a freshwater fish of the carp family.

indicators.note: inside places the letter for left within the word for supports

parts.note: piers are pillars that support a bridge

explanation.surface: A tool has been left among the pillars.
explanation.definitionFit: Pliers are a gripping hand tool, an instrument for holding or bending.

parts.note: aired means broadcast or made public
ale is a type of beer

explanation.surface: A dog breed is advertised alongside a beer.
explanation.definitionFit: The Airedale is a large terrier breed from Yorkshire, so it is a kind of dog.

clue.text: Return weapon to obtain something small and valuable

indicators.note: return signals that the weapon word is turned round and read backwards

parts.note: a gun is a weapon
to get is to obtain

explanation.surface: Bringing back a weapon to obtain a little treasure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Return' turns GUN into NUG.
explanation.definitionFit: A nugget is a small lump of gold, or figuratively a precious titbit of information.

parts.note: to hamper is to hinder or hold up

explanation.surface: A Tory delays a drinks order, speaking informally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'commonly' marks the slang: champers is informal British for champagne.
explanation.definitionFit: Champers is British slang for champagne, the sparkling wine.
